chunks: And what Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Isma'il who said: Abu al-Hasan ibn Zarif narrated to me from Tha'labah from Aban from Ibn Abi Ya'fur who said:

I asked him about what is prohibited through breastfeeding. He said: 'When the infant breastfeeds until its belly is full, for that causes flesh and blood to grow, and that is what prohibits [marriage].'

Therefore, these two reports do not contradict what we have previously mentioned, because there is no conflict between his statement that 'fifteen consecutive sucklings prohibit,' and his statement that 'it is when he breastfeeds until he is full and his self/soul is satisfied,' and between his statement 'breastfeeding of a day and a night,' because these three are limits expressing what causes flesh to grow and bone to strengthen. Whichever one knowledge establishes, the prohibition is known by it, and there is no contradiction among them in any respect.
As for what was narrated - Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar from Ali ibn Mahziyar from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him)
He wrote to him asking him about what is prohibited through breastfeeding, so he (peace be upon him) wrote back: 'Its little and its much are prohibited.'

Therefore, this report is understood to mean that its little and its much are prohibited after it reaches the limit that prohibits or exceeds it, for whether the addition is little or much, it prohibits. And it is permissible that it came out as Taqiyya (dissimulation), because it agrees with the view of some of the Sunnis.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on breastfeeding establishing prohibition in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi synthesizes seemingly contradictory narrations by identifying the underlying physiological cause of prohibition—sufficient nourishment leading to flesh and bone growth—rather than adhering strictly to numerical counts. He further contextualizes the report stating 'little and much is prohibited' as either referring to the period after the threshold is met or as an instance of *taqiyya* (dissimulation) to align with Sunni jurisprudence, demonstrating the Shia method of harmonizing textual evidence with practical legal realities.
